body:
The current version of the Application Security Verification Standard (ASVS) does not include a specific verification item for preventing loop bound injection attacks, which is a security vulnerability that can occur in code that uses loops to iterate over data and can cause a DoS. Therefore, it is recommended to add a new verification item to help ensure that developers take appropriate steps to prevent this type of vulnerability.
Please check this [reference](https://codeql.github.com/codeql-query-help/javascript/js-loop-bound-injection/) to see sample vulnerable codes (the attacker can modify the length property without inserting any items into the object).

A sample check could be this one:
_Verify that input validation is performed for all loop conditions to prevent loop bound injection attacks._

comments.body:
The name "loop bound injection" is confusing for me.

The actual context is basically just input validation, and if it's not done, then as an impact in some context it may cause "running out of resources". "Loop" means it actually never ends, but based on description, it's not the case here.

Now there is question, do we want to have separate requirement to say - Verify that your input validation rules are matching with available resources.

Similar requirements already exists in business logic and file handling area:
| # | Description | L1 | L2 | L3 | CWE |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **11.1.3** | Verify the application has appropriate limits for specific business actions or transactions which are correctly enforced on a per user basis. | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | 770 |
| **11.1.5** | Verify the application has business logic limits or validation to protect against likely business risks or threats, identified using threat modeling or similar methodologies. | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | 841 |
| **12.1.1** | [MODIFIED] Verify that the application will only accept files of a size which it can process without causing a loss of performance or denial of service attack. | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | 400 |
| **12.1.3** | Verify that a file size quota and maximum number of files per user is enforced to ensure that a single user cannot fill up the storage with too many files, or excessively large files. | | ✓ | ✓ | 770 |

In a way related: https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/934
(if someone can ask too many rows/too big response to the output, that server can not produce it - running out of memory)
Well, "attacker can modify" .. how? What is the precondition that an attacker can do that?

I checked it before I wrote my first comment. I still think it's input validation question with different potential outcome as impact.

For JSON and for this example we need to meet the requirement 13.2.2 first:
_13.2.2 | Verify that JSON schema validation is in place and verified before accepting input._

At same time I'm opened to point-of-views, how it is not (only) an input validation question.

I believe JSON schema validation alone may not be sufficient to prevent loop bound injection attacks. Also, there are many ASVS items that can be grouped into one ASVS item under the name of input validation (all injection related attaks) but we have not done that (which is good). The point here is to make the tester aware of this attack vector.

> Also, there are many ASVS items that can be grouped into one ASVS item under the name of input validation (all injection related attaks) but we have not done that (which is good).

A bit offtopic, but - against injection attack you need mostly encoding, then sanitization, then input validation.

> The point here is to make the tester aware of this attack vector.

Yes, awareness is good. The question - is ASVS the correct project to achieve it (if the reason is only awareness)?

And back to the beginning: can you provide an example - how _loop bound injection_ can happen if input validation (including JSON schema validation) is done correctly?

Where I want to reach is - if it's not a separate and independent problem, then I'm not sure it's worth separate and independent requirement. Note: I'm not sure does not mean I'm against that.

Actually you do •not• need encoding, injection or sanitization for the most severe form of injection. You need query parameterization to stop SQL injection.This is why injection is a lot more difficult to fix than most people think because each individual type of injection has a very different formula for how it needs to be fixed.
If the developer uses maxItems in the JSON Schema to set a bound we can prevent this attack, should we rephrase the ASVS item to mention this too?

So this is like a context specific input validation. I mean that it is not sufficient to check that the data is the right type, size or format for the target type but that it is a valid value for this particular case. So this could potentially be a general requirement about context specific input validation.

On the other hand, maybe we need to specifically mandate context specific input validation where input is affecting control flow.
- @ImanSharaf @elarlang What do you think?
- @elarlang do we have a catch-all label for input validation re-write yet? If not, do you think we need one?

I think the control flow thing here is the key point. I would propose an addition to V5.1 Input Validation:

| # | Description | L1 | L2 | L3 | CWE |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **5.1.7** | [ADDED] Verify that untrusted input which can affect control flow (such as the number of iterations in a loop) is carefully validated against expectations. | | ✓ | ✓ | |
@ImanSharaf @elarlang comments?
Can you clarify, what is the risk or attack vector to solve with this?

This is the attack vector which concerns me:
